transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapur (Redwood SE), Avinash Rao (Redwood Product), Mark Delgado (Zenith CTO), Sofia Ramos (Zenith Head of AI), Liam O'Connell (Zenith DevOps), Tessa Wu (Zenith PM)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff patterns, idempotency and rate limits. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a customer-facing assistant with strict latency requirements and some data residency concerns. Agreed next steps: pricing & POC scoping.

Topics Covered:
- Hosted API intro and model catalog
- Streaming vs non-streaming responses
- Parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences)
- Retries, exponential backoff, idempotency keys
- SDK examples + cURL examples
- Rate limits, quotas, and batching implications
- Security: SOC2, SSO, encryption, data retention
- Next steps and POC scope

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan from Redwood. quick roll call?
[00:08] Mark Delgado: Mark here, CTO at Zenith. Sofia, Liam, Tessa on our side.
[00:12] Sofia Ramos: hi all, Sofia.
[00:14] Jordan Lee: Awesome. Priya and Avinash from our side as well. We're gonna run through a hosted API demo — chat and text generation basics — and leave time for questions, especially around latency and security. Sound good?
[00:26] Liam O'Connell: yep sounds good. we're mostly concerned about p99 latency under load, and cost, and how retries are handled.
[00:34] Priya Kapur: great—I'll share my screen in a sec, but quick high-level first: hosted API gives you immediate access to our model catalog, streaming, structured outputs, and built-in rate limiting. If you need predictable throughput we can discuss Dedicated.
[00:47] Jordan Lee: also, want to call out our Optimize tooling — later we can show batching and caching suggestions that help drop cost with minimal latency impact.
[00:55] 
[01:10] Priya Kapur: ok sharing — so here's a very basic chat call. cURL or SDK are both supported. the core fields we typically tweak are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and stop sequences. i'll run a simple request to show streaming.
[01:28] Priya Kapur: (typing sounds) here's a streaming response — you can see tokens arrive incrementally. this reduces time-to-first-byte for long replies, and is great for chat UIs.
[01:40] Sofia Ramos: sorry, is streaming enabled by default?
[01:43] Priya Kapur: it's opt-in. you set stream=true. if you don't want partial results you get the full response when complete. streaming can slightly change cost accounting depending on how you count partial tokens in some SDKs, but we surface that in the console.
[02:00] Mark Delgado: what's the behavior on network drop mid-stream? do we resend from start or resume?
[02:06] Priya Kapur: good question. for hosted, depending on client-side SDK you can resume from the last message id using an idempotency token pattern, but we don't currently support byte-range resume of the stream. typical pattern is to use idempotency key per user-message so replays are safe and you detect duplicates server-side.
[02:26] Jordan Lee: another pattern is to cache the generated prefix at the application layer — Redwood supports prefix/KV caching on the runtime which helps if you need very low p99 on repeated prompts.
[02:40] Liam O'Connell: can you explain prefix caching a bit more?
[02:43] Priya Kapur: sure — if many requests share common prompt prefixes (like system instructions or user history), we cache the KV cache for that prefix so subsequent calls only compute the tail. it reduces tokens processed and latency.
[02:58] 
[03:15] Priya Kapur: back to params — temperature controls randomness; 0 is deterministic-ish, higher like 0.8 more creative. top_p is nucleus sampling; often you tune one or the other. max_tokens caps response length. stop sequences help keep outputs constrained.
[03:34] Tessa Wu: for our assistant we want consistent short replies, sometimes a multi-turn summary. what settings do you recommend?
[03:40] Priya Kapur: for consistency start at temperature 0.2–0.4, top_p 0.8–1, and use a hard max_tokens like 150 for short replies. for summaries you can increase max_tokens and keep temperature lower. also instructive system messages help.
[03:58] Mark Delgado: how do retries work if we hit e.g., 429s?
[04:03] Priya Kapur: Redwood recommends exponential backoff with jitter. for idempotent requests include an idempotency key so a retry doesn't create duplicate side effects. our SDK has built-in retry helpers that follow best practices and surface remaining quota info.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: and on 5xxs we also recommend short exponential backoff; we expose retry-after headers when rate limited.
[04:27] 
[04:45] Priya Kapur: I'll switch to a quick code example — here's JS SDK usage: create a request with messages, set stream true, attach an idempotency key. watch how the client emits 'chunk' events.
[04:58] Sofia Ramos: do you have latency numbers for small models vs larger?
[05:03] Priya Kapur: depends on model and sequence length. for example on our curated medium model p50 is ~60–120ms for 16-token responses; p95/p99 will be higher. larger models can be 2–5x depending on token length. We have per-model perf profiles in the console.
[05:22] 
[05:40] Avinash Rao: to add — the runtime chooses optimized kernels and quantization profiles; we surface a performance profile so you can choose the sweet spot for cost/latency.
[05:50] Liam O'Connell: that perf profile — is it public? can we run our own benchmarks?
[05:55] Priya Kapur: yes, you can run benchmarks. Priya (laughs) — sorry i meant we provide a benchmark script. we'll share a sample script and test credentials for a small trial so you can replicate with your prompts.
[06:08] Jordan Lee: we'll also include a spreadsheet showing tokens per call, expected monthly cost at various QPS, and options for reserved capacity if you want lower unit costs.
[06:18] 
[06:35] Mark Delgado: a couple of security questions: SOC2? where data is stored? can we get network diagrams?
[06:42] Jordan Lee: Redwood is SOC2 Type II compliant — we'll share the report under NDA. For hosted, data is stored in region you select; we support encryption at rest with customer-managed keys via KMS in Dedicated/Private options. We'll share network diagrams and our security whitepaper.
[07:00] Sofia Ramos: do you do any training or retention of customer prompts?
[07:05] Priya Kapur: by default hosted API logs requests for troubleshooting and quality monitoring; retention policies can be configured and enterprise customers can opt out of retention or use Private deployment if you need zero retention. We have redact and PII filters as well.
[07:20] 
[07:40] Liam O'Connell: what's the onboarding like for SSO and RBAC?
[07:44] Avinash Rao: SAML SSO is supported; RBAC with fine-grained roles in the Console. Audit logs are available for Dedicated and Private with longer retention as an add-on.
[07:56] 
[08:10] Priya Kapur: back to demo — here's an example of retry logic in Python using the SDK. notice we wrap the request in a retry decorator and pass the idempotency key; the SDK will not retry non-idempotent calls by default.
[08:28] Tessa Wu: you mentioned batching — how does automatic batching interact with user session state?
[08:34] Priya Kapur: automatic batching is request-level and works best for stateless or similar short prompts. for multi-turn chat where history matters you can still batch but we'd batch tails with similar prefixes, and caching helps there. you can also set per-route batching sizes in the Console.
[08:52] 
[09:10] Mark Delgado: cost controls — can we set hard quotas per team or route?
[09:14] Jordan Lee: yes, Console supports per-token quotas, per-route limits, and alerts. you can also enforce model whitelists so teams can't spin up large models without approval.
[09:26] 
[09:45] Priya Kapur: demoing the Console now — here's a route configuration: choose model, streaming on/off, max concurrency, batching policy. Notice the per-route latency and cost estimates on the right.
[10:00] Sofia Ramos: is there an API to manage routes programmatically?
[10:03] Priya Kapur: yes, same API surface; routes are first-class via our management API. we can also do canary rollouts and A/B tests.
[10:15] 
[10:30] Jordan Lee: quick note about consistency — if you need strict p99 SLOs and guaranteed capacity, Dedicated is usually the path. Hosted is great for quick time-to-value and many customers run production on hosted, but if you have predictable high QPS and need isolation, Dedicated or Private make sense.
[10:51] Mark Delgado: for our target 200 qps peak with p99 < 600ms for short replies, would you recommend Hosted or Dedicated?
[11:00] Priya Kapur: we'd run a benchmark with your prompt set. Many customers at that volume start with hosted trial — we can provision higher-tier instances or reserved capacity. If sustained, Dedicated reduces cost and gives more predictable latency.
[11:14] 
[11:30] Liam O'Connell: any recommendations for minimizing token usage?
[11:34] Priya Kapur: yes — prompt engineering to shorten context, use KV/prefix caching for repeated system prompts, and compressing user history (summaries) before sending. Also the Optimize tool recommends quantization/model tradeoffs and batching parameters.
[11:50] 
[12:05] Priya Kapur: i'll demonstrate a streaming error scenario — intentionally throttle the client, you'll see a 429 with retry-after header. SDK surfaces that header and our client helper waits and retries with jitter.
[12:20] Mark Delgado: do you have SLA language around rate limits or ooms?
[12:24] Jordan Lee: our hosted SLA covers availability and we have rate-limit policies that are tiered. For guaranteed throughput, Dedicated has contractual SLAs. we'll include SLA excerpts in the docs we send.
[12:39] 
[12:55] Priya Kapur: another operational tip — attach request metadata (app id, user id) and we expose token-level cost per request in the Console which helps show where your spend is coming from.
[13:10] Tessa Wu: great, that helps product teams allocate cost back to features.
[13:14] 
[13:30] Sofia Ramos: about model updates — what's the versioning story?
[13:34] Avinash Rao: models are versioned in the catalog and you can pin a version on a route. we support canary and A/B rollouts and quality monitoring tied to your eval sets so you can detect regressions.
[13:48] 
[14:05] Mark Delgado: ok, anything on regional data residency? we have EU users and need some EU-only constraints.
[14:12] Jordan Lee: yes, you can select region for hosted; for strict residency or legal controls we recommend Private or Dedicated with region-specific deployments. we'll share a region map.
[14:27] 
[14:45] Priya Kapur: quick recaps from the demo: streaming = faster partial delivery, params control randomness and length, use idempotency keys + exponential backoff for reliable retries, prefix caching and batching to reduce cost/latency, Console has per-route controls and Optimize suggests config changes.
[15:05] Mark Delgado: sounds good. any rough timelines for a POC?
[15:09] Jordan Lee: we can get you trial API keys and a small reserved pool within a week; full POC scoping call next week to lock test dataset and acceptance criteria.
[15:18] Sofia Ramos: we'll want Priya to run a latency run with our prompts and 200 qps shape if possible.
[15:24] Priya Kapur: yes, we'll do that — ideally you upload a representative prompt file and we run both burst and sustained profiles.
[15:32] Tessa Wu: who should we send the sample prompts to?
[15:35] Jordan Lee: I'll follow up with an email and a shared folder link. Mark, Sofia — please put the prompt set there.
[15:42] 
[15:55] Mark Delgado: thanks. last quick question — do you support function/tool calling for structured outputs?
[16:00] Avinash Rao: yes, we support tool/function calling patterns and structured JSON outputs, with schema enforcement in the SDKs. good for extraction tasks.
[16:12] 
[16:30] Jordan Lee: ok we'll wrap with next steps — I'll send pricing and the SOC2/network diagrams under NDA, Priya will share a benchmark script and we target a POC scoping call on 2026-03-20.
[16:44] Sofia Ramos: thanks everyone.
[16:46] Liam O'Connell: thanks.
[16:48] Jordan Lee: thanks all — end.

End of transcript.
